text.p: The old and new faces of German tennis made significant progress at Wimbledon on Tuesday before rain returned to halt a delicately-poised men's fourth round.

Former champion Michael Stich, Britain's Greg Rusedski and France's Cedric Pioline were the only players definitely through to the last eight when a heavy shower intervened, but Boris Becker and teenager Nicolas Kiefer were both poised to swell the list of German representation.

Becker cruised through the first two sets against ninth seed Marcelo Rios and, although the Chilean held a 3-0 lead in the third when play was stopped, the three-time champion looked a certainty to go through.
Kiefer, one of the first two players to be accepted into the recently-formed Becker junior team in Germany, was also on the brink of a quarter-final place on his first senior visit to Wimbledon.
The 19-year-old led world number three Yevgeny Kafelnikov 6-2 7-5 2-6 3-1, confirming the good impression he made in beating Andrei Medvedev in the previous round.
Stich's decision to retire later this year emphasises the changing times in German tennis, but the 1991 champion remains a dangerous customer on grass.
He knocked out Australia's Mark Woodforde 6-4 6-7 6-3 7-5 and will not be a pushover for either Tim Henman or defending champion Richard Krajicek in the quarter-finals.
Britain already have one man in the last eight and the Canadian-reared Rusedski is serving well enough to worry anyone.
He thundered down 12 aces in the first set alone against American Richey Reneberg and his 7-6 6-4 7-6 victory was his third straight sets win in four matches.
"That was one of the best matches I've ever served," he said, before acknowledging there was still a lot of hard work to be done. "If I hit aces that's good, but I'd much rather win matches."
His quarter-final opponent will be Frenchman Cedric Pioline, who reached the last eight for the third time in five years with a 3-6 6-3 6-4 7-5 win over New Zealander Brett Steven.
No-one earned a bigger cheer, however, than Stefan Edberg who was given a minute-long standing ovation on Centre Court in recognition of his contribution to Wimbledon over the years.
